subject: 4B803FE7ECD54DB8A0941F918BB42943
introduction: “The Ancient Beauty hath consented to be bound with chains that mankind may be released from its bondage.” Bahá’u’lláh’s writings say of His own imprisonment and exile what Christians say of the cross: that it was accepted for the life, freedom and renewal of the world. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s talks then explain what such a sacrifice does. It is “an example”, it educates, it shows that there are worlds beyond this one, and it calls for the sacrifice of the lower self in return. The New Testament supplies the nearest language, the good shepherd, the corn of wheat, “a ransom for many”, “for your sakes he became poor”, and Isaiah’s suffering servant stands behind both. The contrary voices matter here. Ezekiel and the Qur’an deny that one soul can bear another’s burden; Hebrews insists on blood where ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of example; and the Qur’an’s “they slew him not” is the verse on which Muslim and Christian accounts of Jesus divide. Gibbon on Ḥusayn and Dickens’s Sydney Carton show the hold of such deaths on those outside the faith concerned.
questions: In what sense do the readings say the Manifestation’s suffering “redeems”? Collect the verbs they use (release, regenerate, educate, draw nigh) and compare them with “ransom”.
Ezekiel and the Qur’an say no one bears another’s load. Is the readings’ account of sacrifice open to that objection?
Reading 34 has Christ say “I offer myself as an example”. What does an example accomplish that a teaching does not?
Reading 42 names a second redemption, giving up the self. How is the believer’s response part of what the sacrifice achieves?
Why do the deaths of Ḥusayn, of Christ, of the Báb continue to move people centuries later, including those who do not share the faith?

outside.why: Bound with chains that mankind may be released. He hath sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound.
Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
Because He bore injustice, justice has appeared. He was wounded for our transgressions; the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
By sacrificing Himself, a fresh capacity was infused into all things. Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
Why the Manifestations endure every calamity. God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.
A captive in chains or under a sword all His days. He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
That every one of you may become a source of goodness. He bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness.
“He hath sacrificed His spirit out of love.” The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
“We have offered up Our soul for the love of God and for the life of the worlds.” Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
“We have desired naught for Ourselves, but rather for your sakes.” While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
What was borne for the liberation of Thy servants. Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
He accepted abasement for the glory of all. The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
Imprisoned for the emancipation of the world. Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free.
Adversity accepted “to regenerate all that are in Thy heaven and on Thy earth”. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.

“Offered up as a ransom.” Ezekiel denies that one can pay for another: the soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. How do the readings understand “ransom”? See 34, 40 and 41.
The Qur’an agrees with Ezekiel: each soul earneth only on its own account, nor doth any laden bear another’s load.
“My son bloodstained before Thy face.” Abraham, with his son on the way to the mountain: God will provide himself a lamb.
“O Husayn! Hearken unto the call of this Husayn.” Gibbon, no friend to religion: in a distant age and climate, the tragic scene of the death of Hosein will awaken the sympathy of the coldest reader.
The deeds of the Prophets show there are worlds besides this. They wandered in deserts and in mountains: of whom the world was not worthy.
He knew what proclaiming Himself would cost. Who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame.

Christ said in substance, “I offer myself as an example”, where the old custom offered sacrifices for sins. Hebrews keeps the older logic: without shedding of blood is no remission. The reading turns atonement into example and education. What is kept of the traditional doctrine, and what is set aside?
The prophets had already begun the turn from ritual sacrifice that the reading describes: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.

Some die for their crimes; He died for others. Caiaphas said more than he meant: it is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not. What is the difference between a sacrifice offered and a scapegoat taken?
If physical life mattered most, Christ would not have accepted the cross. What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
Every Manifestation knows he will be destroyed. O Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee.
His self-sacrifice gave believers eternal life. I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved.
As the sheep gave its life, the animal nature must be sacrificed. Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God.
Two redemptions: giving the life, and giving up the self. If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross.
Had Christ not been sacrificed, there would be no spring. Tertullian wrote in the age when it was still happening: straightway the cry is, Away with the Christians to the lion!
“Fighting even upon the cross”, and victorious through the centuries. Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.

He sacrificed himself for all mankind. Dickens gave the words to a wasted man dying in another’s place: it is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done. Why does such a death move people who hold no doctrine about it?

The Báb’s martyrdom and Bahá’u’lláh’s sufferings. The Qur’an on the cross: they slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them. Muslims have generally taken this to deny the crucifixion that the readings treat as the model sacrifice. How do the readings’ words about spirit and body bear on the verse?
He suffered all this “for us, that we may turn to God”. God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself; be ye reconciled to God.
The response the guide ends on: we love him, because he first loved us.

shortfall: Readings 8 to 27 state one thought (He accepted suffering for your deliverance) in twenty short sentences, and 45 to 49 repeat it of Bahá’u’lláh; a companion was given to each form of it once.

peter-by-whose-stripes.text: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed

john-one-man-should-die-for-the-people.text: And one of them, named Caiaphas, being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all, Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not

hebrews-without-shedding-of-blood.text: And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission
